title: When Self-Improvement Becomes Self-Rejection

reels.hook: Two men at the gym at 6 a.m.
reels.hook_b: Same gym. Same programme. Only one of them lasts.
cards: Two men at the gym at 6 a.m.

ONE
He wants to be strong for the next forty years.

THE OTHER
He can't stand what he sees in the mirror.
Self-critical people made less progress on their goals, not more.
Which one got up this morning?
reels.visual: V3 empty gym at dawn, rack and bench, no people (tag gym-dawn), else V1 + grain.
reels.caption:
Two men, same programme, same alarm. One is building something. The other is serving a sentence.

Across five studies, people higher in self-criticism made less progress on their goals, including less weight loss over six months. It's correlational, but it's the opposite of what the inner critic promises.

Which one is getting up in you?

Evidence: Powers et al. (2011). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: Building or serving a sentence? One word.

reels.hook: Would you talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself?
reels.hook_b: You'd never talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself.
cards: Would you talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself?
People nudged to be kind to themselves about a weakness…
…were more motivated to fix it, not less.
Tonight: write to yourself the way you'd write to them.
Honest about the problem. Kind about the person.
Save this for the next bad week.
reels.visual: V2 own clip of a pen and an open letter pad under a lamp (tag letter-lamp), else V1 + grain.
reels.evidence: Tier 1 experiments (E20; design via secondary summary, check before scheduling) + Moodius practice
reels.caption:
Most people who are hard on themselves think it's what keeps them going.

In four experiments, people nudged towards self-compassion about a weakness, a mistake or a failed test were more motivated to improve, not less.

Try this tonight: write to yourself about the thing you're trying to change, the way you'd write to a friend who was struggling with it. Honest about the problem, kind about the person.

What would that letter say?

Evidence: Breines & Chen (2012). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: What would a friend say to you about the thing you're working on?

carousel: Improving yourself and rejecting yourself can look exactly the same.
Here's how to tell the difference →
Socially prescribed perfectionism rose about 33% among students from 1989 to 2016.
Self-critical people made less progress on goals, including less weight loss over six months.
Studies · Powers et al., PSPB (2011) · correlational
People nudged to self-compassion were more motivated to improve, not less.
"Be not disgusted, nor discouraged, nor dissatisfied, if thou dost not succeed in doing everything according to right principles."
A missed day feels like evidence · You're escaping, not heading somewhere · Progress brings relief, not satisfaction
Reject the behaviour. Keep the person.
Full essay on the Substack · link in bio · save this
carousel_caption:
Self-improvement can run on care or on contempt. From outside they look identical.

The research suggests the contempt version works worse: self-criticism went with less progress, and self-compassion with more motivation to improve. High standards aren't the problem. What you do with a bad week is.

Which fuel are you running on?

Evidence: Curran & Hill 2019; Powers et al. 2011; Breines & Chen 2012; Neff 2003. Philosophy: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.9 (Long).
notes: Most people who are hard on themselves believe it's what keeps them going. In five studies, self-critical people made less progress on their goals, not more, including measured weight loss over six months. The inner critic's promise doesn't seem to hold.

Marcus Aurelius, to himself: don't be disgusted or discouraged if you don't manage to do everything by your principles; when you fail, come back. The Stoics get recruited as patron saints of grinding discipline. On this, at least, Marcus was gentler with himself than most of the people who quote him.
A test for whether your self-improvement has turned into self-rejection: does a missed day feel like a missed day, or like evidence about who you are? This week's essay is about the difference.
